title: The Trailer Return
primary_metric: deadhead ratio -- total block-segments driven per block-segment actually serviced, for one full recycling collection run across the Bay Fruit Streets grid

options.A: The Closed Loop -- keep Truck 4 driving itself back to the yard every collection day, under today's full closed-circuit (Euler-circuit) repeat mileage
options.B: The Trailer Return -- contract a flatbed hauler to retrieve Truck 4 from wherever its shortest open path (Euler-path) ends, cutting repeat mileage at the cost of a daily hauling fee

Open-path (best pair removed -- Monroe Avenue dead end & north Strawberry Street): 1.1882 mi minimum repeat mileage, 8.5127 mi total driven, deadhead ratio 1.1622. Practice Block excerpt (26 vertices, 37 edges, 2.4636 mi, 14 odd vertices): closed 0.5407 mi repeat, open 0.2482 mi repeat (best pair M/L).
sources.as_of: OSM data as of 2026-09-09 fetch; underlying street geometry is a live, editable dataset
sources.title: Cape Charles, Virginia historic downtown street-network data, retrieved via the Overpass API
sources.note: Raw way/node data fetched for a bounding box (37.2620,-76.0230,37.2720,-76.0100) covering the named-street historic grid, highway types residential/tertiary/unclassified/living_street only. Pipeline: (1) collapsed raw OSM way geometry into a vertex/edge graph -- a vertex is any node shared by 2+ differently-named streets or a true dead end, an edge is the summed haversine-distance length of an uninterrupted same-named run between two such vertices; (2) excluded 4 way segments running toward the marina/highway outside the district (SEE Appendix F MA2); (3) computed vertex degree by counting incident edges; (4) computed the minimum-weight matching of all odd-degree vertices (closed circuit) and, separately, the minimum-weight matching after testing every candidate pair of odd vertices as an unmatched start/end pair and keeping the cheapest (open path), both via networkx's blossom-algorithm min_weight_matching over all-pairs Dijkstra shortest-path distances -- exact optima, not heuristics; (5) extracted a 26-vertex geographic sub-box as the Practice Block and repeated the same computation on it alone. Full script logic and intermediate outputs are recorded in RESEARCH_LOG.md. Data (c) OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL 1.0 (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright).

_ext: keys below are pipeline extensions, additive to SPEC §4
protagonist: Denise Okafor, Recycling Route Coordinator, Department of Public Works, Town of Averyton -- 15 years on the route, keeps a hand-annotated paper street map bungeed to the truck because, in her words, the GPS "argues with her" about one-ways and construction closures and her paper map has never been wrong; practical and a little stubborn about trusting her own field knowledge over software, treats even a few minutes shaved off a route as a real win, not a luddite -- just knows these streets better than any app does
concept_sheet: Session concept: closing/reinforcing discrete-mathematics-how-to-determine-whether-a-graph-has-an-euler-path-or-circuit (n=1 at time of authoring) via a real municipal recycling-collection route, deliberately distinct in setting and dilemma from cases/the-one-pass-route (street-sweeping, Chinese-Postman connector-street construction) and cases/reroute-wait (transit-line bridge closure, shortest-path)

deliverables.text: A vertex-degree table for every corner in the Bay Fruit Streets Practice Block (a real 26-intersection excerpt of the full grid), each vertex labeled EVEN or ODD.
A written Euler determination for the full 68-intersection Bay Fruit Streets grid: does it have an Euler circuit, an Euler path, or neither -- justified by the specific odd-vertex count.
A closed-circuit repeat-mileage computation for the Practice Block: pair every odd vertex with another odd vertex using the shortest-path distance table, and compute the resulting deadhead ratio.

An open-path repeat-mileage computation for the same Practice Block: re-run the pairing, but leave exactly one pair of odd vertices unmatched as start/end, minimizing remaining mileage, then compute and compare the new deadhead ratio.
A cost comparison table for the full grid: total daily diesel cost under Option A versus total daily diesel cost plus the flatbed hauling fee under Option B.

balance.argument_a: On raw daily dollars, Option A is not close: The Closed Loop costs $10.07/day in diesel and nothing else, versus The Trailer Return's $9.70/day in diesel plus a real $115/day hauling fee -- roughly 12x more expensive in total, with no realistic fuel-savings payback horizon at these figures.
balance.argument_b: On the case's own stated primary metric, the deadhead ratio genuinely improves: 1.2069 under The Closed Loop down to 1.1622 under The Trailer Return, a real 3.70% reduction in wasted mileage -- comparable in spirit to this project's own gold-standard close-margin case (SPEC §2) -- achieved by correctly reclassifying the problem from an Euler-circuit requirement to an Euler-path requirement and only leaving the cheapest single pair of odd corners unresolved.
balance.margin_basis: Compare Option A's official deadhead ratio (Appendix D: 1.2069) against Option B's (Appendix D: 1.1622), both computed the same way (total miles driven / total miles serviced) over the same full 68-vertex grid. margin_pct = (1.2069-1.1622)/1.2069 = 3.70%.

cohort_bands.note: Split into two desks -- one builds D1/D3 (closed-circuit Practice Block pairing) fully before seeing D4, the other jumps to D4's open-path pairing directly -- then trade findings before the Data Deep Dive so both groups reconcile the same Appendix D numbers and confront Appendix E's dollar-vs-ratio tension together.
Work D1's Practice Block vertex-degree table together on the board as a warm-up (Appendix B), then split into pairs for D3 (closed pairing) vs D4 (open pairing) rather than four separate desks.

No vote at Anchor 1 -- the learner states an initial position (Closed Loop or Trailer Return), and the guide argues the other side directly. Spend recovered time on D3/D4's odd-vertex pairing using Appendix C's distance table, the step most likely to trip up a solo learner.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: The Bay Fruit Streets grid's identity
modeling_assumptions.value_used: Modeled using the real, public street layout of the historic downtown grid of Cape Charles, Virginia (OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL license) as a structural stand-in for the fictional town of Averyton's Bay Fruit Streets district
modeling_assumptions.basis: Averyton is fictional, so no real street-network data exists for it. Cape Charles is a real, small, historically-platted coastal town with a genuinely irregular grid, and its full network is public and directly downloadable via the Overpass API.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: The entire case depends on this specific real network's actual topology. A different real town would give different numbers, though the qualitative finding reflects a general graph-theory pattern, not an artifact of this one town.

modeling_assumptions.value_used: Old Cape Charles Road, Bayshore Road, Marina Road, and Harbor Street excluded from the grid
modeling_assumptions.basis: These OSM-mapped segments run well past any sensible reading of a compact downtown recycling route, toward the marina and the highway.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Does not change the odd/even parity of any vertex that remains in-district.

modeling_assumptions.value_used: Treated as already flexible near the Public Works yard each morning; only the route's single END corner is optimized between options
modeling_assumptions.basis: The case does not model a specific yard address outside the mapped grid, so it holds the start point constant across both options and lets only the deliberately-relaxed constraint (closed circuit vs. open path) vary.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: If the yard were instead modeled at a fixed, specific corner inside the grid, the exact best open-path pair could shift, though the general qualitative result would not.

modeling_assumptions.value_used: $115 per collection day, Option B only
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public rate exists for a same-day in-town flatbed pickup of a loaded municipal collection truck. 2026 published flatbed-towing rates for a standard vehicle run $75-150 hookup plus $3.50-7.00/mile (S6); this case uses a value near the low end of that hookup range, since the in-town return leg is short.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the swing figure between the two options' raw dollar totals, but the case is not sensitive to its exact direction: even at half this value, the Trailer Return fee remains far larger than the fuel savings it offsets (Appendix E), so Option A's dollar dominance is robust to plausible variation in MA4.

sensitivity_note: This case involves no illness, death, money stress, or family-hardship subject matter beyond an ordinary municipal route-planning memo; SPEC §6 does not require a facilitator flag beyond ordinary care with a case that touches real household service reliability and a town's fuel budget.

catalog.ask: Every single day, a recycling truck drives its own long way back to the yard just to close the loop. Denise thinks there's a shorter path -- if the town is willing to pay someone else to come get the truck instead. Is the shortcut actually worth the extra bill?
